model.opcrime_dashboard.int_incidents_da.raw_code:
-- The definition of a usable incident, in one place.
--
-- Two date classes are excluded from every count the dashboard publishes: the
-- 1900-01-01 sentinel that means the parser could not read a date at all, and
-- dates in the future, which are source typos. Both are kept here and labelled
-- rather than filtered, so the exclusion is countable instead of invisible.
--
-- Mirrors the excluded block in build_aggregates.py.

select
    record_id,
    date_day,

    case
        when date_day <= '{{ var("date_floor") }}' then 'date_sentinel'
        when date_day > current_date then 'date_future'
        else 'usable'
    end as date_class,

    date_day > '{{ var("date_floor") }}' and date_day <= current_date as is_usable,

    -- Before the open-data dashboard stream began, coverage is PDF bulletins
    -- only. Comparisons that straddle this line are not like-for-like.
    date_day >= '{{ var("regime_change_date") }}' as is_post_regime_change

from {{ ref('stg_incidents') }}

model.opcrime_dashboard.int_incident_dar.raw_code:
-- What share of each incident's time window fell in civil darkness.
--
-- This is a faithful port of _dark_fraction in build_aggregates.py, not a
-- reimplementation. The rule there: walk every minute from start_min to
-- start_min + duration, wrap at 1440, and count the minutes before civil dawn
-- or at/after civil dusk. A closed form would be shorter but would have to
-- special-case the wrap, and the point of this model is that it agrees with the
-- published panel exactly.
--
-- Only usable rows with a parsed, non-sentinel time and a calendar date qualify,
-- which is the same filter and the same inner join the Python does. That lands on
-- the row count the SPA prints as time_darkness_rows_used. The is_usable term is
-- stated rather than left to the calendar join: the four rows it removes have
-- dates outside the calendar range anyway, so relying on the join would give the
-- right answer for the wrong reason.

with usable as (
    select
        i.record_id,
        i.date_day,
        i.start_hour * 60 + i.start_minute as start_min,
        i.duration_minutes,
        c.dawn_minutes,
        c.dusk_minutes
    from {{ ref('stg_incidents') }} as i
    join (select record_id, is_usable from {{ ref('int_incidents_dated') }}) as d using (record_id)
    join {{ ref('stg_calendar') }} as c using (date_day)
    where d.is_usable
      and i.time_parsed
      and not i.time_unknown_sentinel
),

-- A zero-length window is a point in time, so it gets one minute checked
-- rather than an empty range.
spread as (
    select
        record_id,
        dawn_minutes,
        dusk_minutes,
        unnest(range(
            start_min,
            start_min + greatest(duration_minutes, 1)
        )) % 1440 as minute_of_day
    from usable
),

scored as (
    select
        record_id,
        avg(case when minute_of_day < dawn_minutes
                   or minute_of_day >= dusk_minutes
                 then 1.0 else 0.0 end) as dark_fraction
    from spread
    group by record_id
)

select
    u.record_id,
    u.date_day,
    u.start_min,
    u.duration_minutes,
    u.dawn_minutes,
    u.dusk_minutes,
    s.dark_fraction,

    -- The share of that whole day that was civil-dark. An offense whose
    -- dark_fraction sits above its baseline happens in the dark more than
    -- chance alone would put it there.
    1.0 - (u.dusk_minutes - u.dawn_minutes) / 1440.0 as day_dark_baseline,
    s.dark_fraction - (1.0 - (u.dusk_minutes - u.dawn_minutes) / 1440.0) as dark_bend

from usable as u
join scored as s using (record_id)

-- Does an offense prefer the dark, beyond the fact that nights are dark?
--

-- witnessed live will read as darker than they were.

    avg(dark_fraction) as avg_dark_fraction,
    avg(day_dark_baseline) as avg_dark_baseline,
    avg(dark_bend) as avg_dark_bend,
    count(*) filter (where dark_fraction = 1.0) as fully_dark_incidents,
    count(*) filter (where dark_fraction = 0.0) as fully_light_incidents,
    avg(duration_minutes) as avg_window_minutes,
    count(*) filter (where duration_minutes = 0) as point_in_time_incidents
from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
where is_usable
  and dark_fraction is not null
  and offense is not null
group by offense
having count(*) >= 25

model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_flag_prevale.raw_code:
-- Every gazetteer flag, unpivoted, with how often it fires.
--
-- The wide table is the right shape for the SPA to filter on and the wrong shape
-- for asking which flags are rare. Unpivoting here answers that in one place
-- without a 49-branch union, and the family prefix in each column name becomes a
-- column of its own.
--
-- Denominator is incidents that have narrative text. A flag can only fire on text
-- that exists, so measuring prevalence over all incidents would understate every
-- flag by the share of narrative-free rows.
--
-- The terms behind each flag are private to the pipeline. Only the names are here.

with unpivoted as (
    unpivot (
        select f.*, i.is_usable, i.has_narrative, i.is_post_regime_change
        from {{ ref('stg_narrative_flags') }} as f
        join {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }} as i using (record_id)
    )
    on columns(* exclude (record_id, gazetteer_version, is_usable, has_narrative, is_post_regime_change))
    into name flag_name value flag_value
),

scored as (
    select
        flag_name,
        case
            when flag_name like 'any_%' then 'rollup'
            when flag_name like 'firearm_terms_%' then 'firearm_terms'
            when flag_name like 'vehicle_mo_%' then 'vehicle_mo'
            when flag_name like 'items_stolen_%' then 'items_stolen'
            when flag_name like 'substances_%' then 'substances'
            when flag_name like 'location_types_%' then 'location_types'
            when flag_name like 'outcome_flags_%' then 'outcome_flags'
            else 'other'
        end as flag_family,
        count(*) filter (where has_narrative) as narratives_scanned,
        count(*) filter (where flag_value and has_narrative) as flag_hits,
        count(*) filter (where flag_value and has_narrative and is_post_regime_change)
            as flag_hits_post_regime
    from unpivoted
    where is_usable
    group by flag_name
)

select
    flag_name,
    flag_family,
    flag_name like 'any_%' as is_rollup,
    narratives_scanned,
    flag_hits,
    flag_hits_post_regime,
    case when narratives_scanned > 0
         then flag_hits * 1.0 / narratives_scanned end as prevalence,
    flag_hits = 0 as never_fires
from scored

model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_incidents_by.description: The 168-cell hour-by-weekday heatmap, weighted the way the published panel weights it.

day_of_week.name: day_of_week
day_of_week.description: Day of week as the incident table numbers it. Used by the hour-by-weekday heatmap.

weighted_incidents.name: weighted_incidents
weighted_incidents.description: Incidents in this cell, with range reports spread evenly across the hours they cover. Summing all 168 cells returns the exact number of timed incidents.

distinct_offenses.name: distinct_offenses
distinct_offenses.description: Distinct offense labels contributing to this cell.

model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_incidents_by.raw_code:
-- The hour-by-weekday heatmap, 168 cells, weighted the way the panel weights it.
--
-- An incident reported as "1500-1800 HRS" did not happen at 15:00. The published
-- heatmap spreads a range uniformly across the hours it covers, so three hours of
-- uncertainty contribute a third of an incident each rather than a whole one to
-- the first hour. Point-in-time reports contribute 1.0.
--
-- Faithful port of _hour_dow_matrix in build_aggregates.py. Spreading per minute
-- and dividing is the same arithmetic as its per-hour weights, and it keeps the
-- overnight wrap in one place.

with usable as (
    select
        record_id,
        day_of_week,
        start_hour * 60 + start_minute as start_min,
        duration_minutes,
        time_is_range,
        offense
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable
      and time_parsed
      and not time_unknown_sentinel
),

points as (
    select day_of_week, start_min // 60 % 24 as hour_of_day, offense, 1.0 as weight
    from usable
    where not time_is_range or duration_minutes = 0
),

ranges as (
    select
        day_of_week,
        (unnest(range(start_min, start_min + duration_minutes)) % 1440) // 60 as hour_of_day,
        offense,
        1.0 / duration_minutes as weight
    from usable
    where time_is_range and duration_minutes > 0
),

combined as (
    select * from points
    union all
    select * from ranges
),

grid as (
    select
        d.dow as day_of_week,
        h.hour_of_day
    from (select unnest(range(0, 7)) as dow) as d
    cross join (select unnest(range(0, 24)) as hour_of_day) as h
)

select
    g.day_of_week,
    g.hour_of_day,
    coalesce(sum(c.weight), 0) as weighted_incidents,
    coalesce(count(distinct c.offense), 0) as distinct_offenses
from grid as g
left join combined as c
    on c.day_of_week = g.day_of_week
   and c.hour_of_day = g.hour_of_day
group by g.day_of_week, g.hour_of_day

-- Incidents per zone per month, with the zone's population carried alongside so
-- a rate can be computed without another join.
--
-- Months with no incidents in a zone are present with a zero. A sparse series
-- plotted as a line implies continuity it does not have.

-- Months come from the spine, not from the incidents. Selecting distinct months
-- out of the data means a month with no incidents anywhere in the village is
-- simply absent, which is the same gap that broke the window functions in
-- agg_offense_trends.
with months as (
    select month_start from {{ ref('int_month_spine') }}
),

zones as (
    select zone_id, zone_name, population from {{ ref('dim_zone') }}
),

grid as (
    select m.month_start, z.zone_id, z.zone_name, z.population
    from months as m cross join zones as z
),

counted as (
    select
        date_trunc('month', date_day)::date as month_start,
        zone_id,
        count(*) as incidents,
        count(*) filter (where any_vehicle_mo) as incidents_vehicle_mo,
        count(*) filter (where outcome_flags_arrest) as incidents_with_arrest,
        avg(dark_fraction) as avg_dark_fraction
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and zone_id is not null
    group by 1, 2
)

select
    g.month_start,
    g.zone_id,
    g.zone_name,
    g.population,
    coalesce(c.incidents, 0) as incidents,
    coalesce(c.incidents_vehicle_mo, 0) as incidents_vehicle_mo,
    coalesce(c.incidents_with_arrest, 0) as incidents_with_arrest,
    c.avg_dark_fraction,
    case when g.population > 0
         then coalesce(c.incidents, 0) * 1000.0 / g.population end
        as incidents_per_1k_residents,
    g.month_start >= '{{ var("regime_change_date") }}' as is_post_regime_change
from grid as g
left join counted as c
    on c.month_start = g.month_start
   and c.zone_id = g.zone_id

-- start of the dataset. A zero after an offense first appears is a real
-- observation: it did not happen that month. A zero before it ever appeared would
-- imply the same thing about a period when the category may not have been in use
-- at all, which the 2022 ingestion change makes a live risk.

    select

        offense,
        count(*) as incidents
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and offense is not null
    group by 1, 2

        on s.month_start >= f.first_month

        g.offense,
        g.month_start,
        g.is_post_regime_change,
        coalesce(m.incidents, 0) as incidents
    from grid as g
    left join monthly as m

model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_time_precisi.raw_code:
-- How precise are the dashboard timestamps really?
--
-- The open-data stream carries an exact occur_datetime, which invites treating it
-- as a real instant. It is not always one. Times pile up on round values far
-- beyond what any real distribution would produce: exactly midnight and exactly
-- noon each carry roughly fifty times the uniform per-minute rate, and every
-- on-the-hour value is elevated.
--
-- Midnight and noon are the signature of a date-only record, or of a form that
-- defaults to 12:00 AM. They are almost certainly not 517 incidents that happened
-- at the same instant.
--
-- One row per distinct time-of-day value that clears the clustering threshold, so
-- the reader can see the shape rather than take the caveat on trust.

with timed as (
    select cast(occur_datetime as time) as time_of_day
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable
      and occur_datetime is not null
),

totals as (
    select
        count(*) as timestamped_incidents,
        count(*) / 1440.0 as uniform_per_minute
    from timed
),

counted as (
    select time_of_day, count(*) as incidents
    from timed
    group by time_of_day
)

select
    c.time_of_day,
    date_part('hour', c.time_of_day) as hour_of_day,
    date_part('minute', c.time_of_day) as minute_of_hour,
    c.incidents,
    t.timestamped_incidents,
    c.incidents / t.uniform_per_minute as times_uniform_rate,
    date_part('minute', c.time_of_day) = 0 as is_on_the_hour,
    c.time_of_day in ('00:00:00', '12:00:00') as is_midnight_or_noon
from counted as c
cross join totals as t
where c.incidents >= t.uniform_per_minute * 3

model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_weather_coho.raw_code:
-- Mean incidents per day inside each weather cohort, against the all-days mean.
--
-- These cohorts are NOT a partition. A day can be rainy and cold and windy at
-- once, so the rows here overlap and their day counts do not sum to the number
-- of days in range. Anything that adds these rows together is wrong. Each row is
-- only comparable to the baseline row, never to its siblings.
--
-- The denominator is days, not incidents, and it comes from dim_date so that
-- days with zero incidents are counted. A cohort mean computed over only the
-- days something happened would read high for every cohort.

with days as (
    select * from {{ ref('dim_date') }}
    where not missing_weather
      and date_day <= current_date
),

baseline as (
    select
        'all_days' as cohort,
        'baseline' as cohort_kind,
        count(*) as days,
        sum(incidents) as incidents,
        avg(incidents) as mean_incidents_per_day,
        avg(avg_dark_fraction) as mean_dark_fraction
    from days
),

cohorts as (
    select 'rainy' as cohort, 'precipitation' as cohort_kind, * from days where is_rainy
    union all
    select 'snowy', 'precipitation', * from days where is_snowy
    union all
    select 'hot', 'temperature', * from days where is_hot
    union all
    select 'cold', 'temperature', * from days where is_cold
    union all
    select 'freezing', 'temperature', * from days where is_freezing
    union all
    select 'holiday', 'calendar', * from days where is_holiday
    union all
    select 'weekend', 'calendar', * from days where is_weekend
),

summarised as (
    select
        cohort,
        cohort_kind,
        count(*) as days,
        sum(incidents) as incidents,
        avg(incidents) as mean_incidents_per_day,
        avg(avg_dark_fraction) as mean_dark_fraction
    from cohorts
    group by cohort, cohort_kind
),

combined as (
    select * from baseline
    union all
    select * from summarised
)

select
    c.cohort,
    c.cohort_kind,
    c.days,
    c.incidents,
    c.mean_incidents_per_day,
    c.mean_dark_fraction,
    b.mean_incidents_per_day as baseline_mean_incidents_per_day,
    c.mean_incidents_per_day - b.mean_incidents_per_day as lift_vs_baseline,
    case when b.mean_incidents_per_day > 0
         then c.mean_incidents_per_day / b.mean_incidents_per_day - 1.0 end
        as lift_pct_vs_baseline,
    c.cohort <> 'all_days' as cohorts_overlap
from combined as c
cross join baseline as b

-- Does dbt agree with what the front end printed?
--
-- build_aggregates.py computes in pandas and writes the published JSON. These
-- models recompute the same things from the same artifacts in SQL. Where the two
-- agree, a published number is corroborated by an independent implementation
-- rather than merely asserted. Where they do not, one of them is wrong, and this
-- names which measure to look at.
--
-- Two kinds of check, and the difference matters:
--
--   count  a row count. Cheap, and catches a filter that drifted.
--   value  the output of a rule that had to be reimplemented, compared number
--          for number. This is the one that actually tests a port.
--
-- Counts alone are a weak check. The heatmap weighting and the darkness fraction
-- are both transformations that can be badly wrong while conserving every count:
-- move weight between hours, or mis-wrap an overnight window, and the row count
-- is identical. Only comparing the values catches that.
--
-- Value rows carry a tolerance, because the published JSON rounds. The darkness
-- panel rounds to three decimals and the heatmap to two, so those are the floors
-- below which a difference means nothing.

with published as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_coverage_summary') }}
),

recounted as (
    select
        count(*) as total_rows,
        count(*) filter (where is_usable) as valid_rows,
        count(*) filter (where date_class = 'date_sentinel') as year_1900_sentinel,
        count(*) filter (where date_class = 'date_future') as future_dates
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_dated') }}
),

zones as (
    select
        count(*) filter (where i.zone_id is not null) as zone_assigned_rows,
        count(*) filter (where i.zone_id is null) as zone_unassigned_rows
    from {{ ref('stg_incidents') }} as i
    join {{ ref('int_incidents_dated') }} as d using (record_id)
    where d.is_usable
),

darkness as (
    select count(*) as time_darkness_rows_used
    from {{ ref('int_incident_darkness') }}
),

days as (
    select
        (select count(*) from {{ ref('stg_calendar') }}) as calendar_days,
        (select count(*) from {{ ref('stg_weather_daily') }}) as weather_days_used
),

counts as (
    select 'total_rows' as measure, p.total_rows::double as published_value,
           r.total_rows::double as dbt_value
    from published as p cross join recounted as r
    union all
    select 'valid_rows', p.valid_rows, r.valid_rows
    from published as p cross join recounted as r
    union all
    select 'year_1900_sentinel', p.year_1900_sentinel, r.year_1900_sentinel
    from published as p cross join recounted as r
    union all
    select 'future_dates', p.future_dates, r.future_dates
    from published as p cross join recounted as r
    union all
    select 'zone_assigned_rows', p.zone_assigned_rows, z.zone_assigned_rows
    from published as p cross join zones as z
    union all
    select 'zone_unassigned_rows', p.zone_unassigned_rows, z.zone_unassigned_rows
    from published as p cross join zones as z
    union all
    select 'time_darkness_rows_used', p.time_darkness_rows_used, k.time_darkness_rows_used
    from published as p cross join darkness as k
    union all
    select 'calendar_days', p.calendar_days, d.calendar_days
    from published as p cross join days as d
    union all
    select 'weather_days_used', p.weather_days_used, d.weather_days_used
    from published as p cross join days as d
),

-- Value checks. The overall darkness figures compare directly.
dark_overall as (
    select
        pd.published_dark_fraction,
        pd.published_baseline,
        pd.published_bend,
        (select avg(dark_fraction) from {{ ref('int_incident_darkness') }}) as dbt_fraction,
        (select avg(day_dark_baseline) from {{ ref('int_incident_darkness') }}) as dbt_baseline,
        (select avg(dark_bend) from {{ ref('int_incident_darkness') }}) as dbt_bend
    from {{ ref('stg_published_darkness') }} as pd
    where pd.offense = '__overall__'
),

-- Per-offense darkness collapses to its worst disagreement, so one row says
-- whether any of the ten published offenses drifted.
dark_by_offense as (
    select
        max(abs(p.published_dark_fraction - a.avg_dark_fraction)) as max_fraction_diff,
        count(*) filter (where p.published_incidents <> a.incidents) as count_mismatches,
        count(*) as compared
    from {{ ref('stg_published_darkness') }} as p
    join {{ ref('agg_darkness_by_offense') }} as a on a.offense = p.offense
    where p.offense <> '__overall__'
),

-- Same for the 168 heatmap cells. A total that matches proves nothing about
-- where the weight landed, so the cells are compared individually.
heatmap as (
    select
        max(abs(p.published_weight - a.weighted_incidents)) as max_cell_diff,
        count(*) filter (where abs(p.published_weight - a.weighted_incidents) > 0.01) as cells_off,
        count(*) as compared
    from {{ ref('stg_published_heatmap') }} as p
    join {{ ref('agg_incidents_by_hour_dow') }} as a
        on a.day_of_week = p.day_of_week
       and a.hour_of_day = p.hour_of_day
),

values_ as (
    select 'darkness_overall_fraction' as measure,
           published_dark_fraction as published_value, dbt_fraction as dbt_value
    from dark_overall
    union all
    select 'darkness_overall_baseline', published_baseline, dbt_baseline from dark_overall
    union all
    select 'darkness_overall_bend', published_bend, dbt_bend from dark_overall
    union all
    select 'darkness_by_offense_max_diff', 0.0, max_fraction_diff from dark_by_offense
    union all
    select 'darkness_by_offense_count_mismatches', 0.0, count_mismatches from dark_by_offense
    union all
    select 'heatmap_max_cell_diff', 0.0, max_cell_diff from heatmap
    union all
    select 'heatmap_cells_beyond_tolerance', 0.0, cells_off from heatmap
),

combined as (
    select measure, 'count' as check_kind, published_value, dbt_value, 0.0 as tolerance
    from counts
    union all
    select measure, 'value', published_value, dbt_value,
           case
               when measure like 'heatmap_max_cell_diff' then 0.011
               when measure like 'heatmap_cells_beyond_tolerance' then 0.0
               when measure like 'darkness_by_offense_count_mismatches' then 0.0
               else 0.0011
           end
    from values_
)

select
    measure,
    check_kind,
    published_value,
    dbt_value,
    tolerance,
    abs(dbt_value - published_value) as difference,
    abs(dbt_value - published_value) <= tolerance as agrees
from combined

-- Characteristics: numbers that surprise people and are nonetheless correct.
--
-- These are the questions that get asked about the dataset every time someone new
-- looks at it. Answering them here, next to the defect list rather than inside it,
-- is the point: a third of incidents having no topic is not a bug, it is what
-- happens when a third of incidents arrive without narrative text.
--
-- Classes overlap on purpose and do not sum to the row count.

with rows_all as (
    select * from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
),

totals as (
    select
        count(*) as all_rows,
        count(*) filter (where is_usable) as usable_rows
    from rows_all
),

facts as (
    select 'usable_rows' as characteristic, count(*) as row_count,
        'Rows that survive the date filters and back every published count.' as detail
    from rows_all where is_usable
    union all
    select 'source_pdf_only', count(*),
        'Only the PDF activity bulletin reported this incident.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and source = 'pdf'
    union all
    select 'source_dashboard_only', count(*),
        'Only the open-data dashboard reported it. Mostly post-2022, and the reason both streams exist.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and source = 'dashboard'
    union all
    select 'source_both', count(*),
        'Both streams reported it and upstream merged them on the complaint number.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and source = 'both'
    union all
    select 'has_narrative', count(*),
        'Rows with narrative text. Everything downstream of language, topics and flags alike, can only see these.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and has_narrative
    union all
    select 'no_narrative', count(*),
        'Rows with no narrative. Dashboard-only incidents arrive as structured NIBRS charges with no prose.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and not has_narrative
    union all
    select 'topic_assigned', count(*),
        'Narratives BERTopic placed in a theme, noise bucket included.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and topic_id is not null
    union all
    select 'topic_noise', count(*),
        'Narratives BERTopic declined to cluster. A real answer about the text, not a failure.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and is_noise_topic
    union all
    select 'topic_unassigned', count(*),
        'No topic row at all, because there was no narrative to embed.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and topic_id is null
    union all
    select 'zone_assigned', count(*),
        'Incidents inside one of the eight policing zone polygons.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and zone_id is not null
    union all
    select 'zone_unassigned', count(*),
        'Geocoded outside every zone polygon, or not geocoded at all. An Oak Park address on a boundary street can land just outside.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and zone_id is null
    union all
    select 'time_window_is_range', count(*),
        'Reported as a span rather than a moment. The heatmap spreads these across the hours they cover.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and time_is_range
    union all
    select 'time_unknown_sentinel', count(*),
        'Time recorded as unknown. Excluded from every hour-of-day and darkness measure.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and time_unknown_sentinel
    union all
    select 'time_overnight_window', count(*),
        'Time window crosses midnight, so the hour arithmetic has to wrap.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and time_is_overnight
    union all
    select 'post_regime_change', count(*),
        'On or after 2022-01-01, when open-data ingestion began. Before that, coverage is PDF bulletins only.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and is_post_regime_change
    union all
    select 'multi_charge_incidents', count(*),
        'NIBRS incidents carrying more than one charge, collapsed upstream into one row with arrays.'
    from rows_all where is_usable and charge_count > 1
)

select
    f.characteristic,
    f.row_count,
    case when t.usable_rows > 0 then f.row_count * 100.0 / t.usable_rows end as pct_of_usable,
    f.detail
from facts as f
cross join totals as t

-- Defects only: things that are wrong and could in principle be fixed.
--
-- Deliberately separate from data_profile_summary, which holds the numbers that
-- are surprising but correct. Mixing the two produces a defect count that grows
-- every time the dataset gets more interesting, which trains everyone to ignore
-- it.
--
-- One row per defect class. The classes are not disjoint: an incident can be both
-- ungeocoded and date-mismatched, so summing incident_count across rows
-- overstates the number of affected incidents. Where a single number is needed,
-- count distinct records, not classes.

with rows_all as (
    select * from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
),

totals as (
    select count(*) as all_rows from rows_all
),

date_defects as (
    select
        'date_sentinel' as defect_class,
        'incident' as grain,
        count(*) as defect_count,
        'The date parser could not read a date at all and fell back to 1900-01-01.' as detail
    from rows_all where date_class = 'date_sentinel'
    union all
    select 'date_future', 'incident', count(*),
        'Reported date is later than today, which means a typo at the source.'
    from rows_all where date_class = 'date_future'
    union all
    select 'pdf_dashboard_date_mismatch', 'incident', count(*),
        'The PDF bulletin and the open-data dashboard disagree on the date by at least a day. Upstream keeps the PDF date and flags the row.'
    from rows_all where date_mismatch
),

geocode_defects as (
    select 'ungeocoded' as defect_class, 'incident' as grain, count(*) as defect_count,
        'No coordinates, so the incident cannot be placed on the map or assigned to a zone.' as detail
    from rows_all where is_usable and lat is null
),

    select 'weather_gap_days' as defect_class, 'day' as grain, count(*) as defect_count,

model.opcrime_dashboard.dim_topic.raw_code:
-- One row per BERTopic cluster, with its display words and what it caught.
--
-- Topic -1 is BERTopic's noise bucket, not a theme. It is kept because the size
-- of it is a real measure of how much narrative text would not cluster, and
-- dropping it here would make the topic shares add to more than the corpus.

with words as (
    select
        topic_id,
        string_agg(word, ', ' order by word_rank) as top_words,
        count(*) as word_count,
        max(weight) as top_word_weight
    from {{ ref('stg_topic_words') }}
    group by topic_id
),

assigned as (
    select
        topic_id,
        count(*) as incidents,
        avg(topic_prob) as avg_topic_prob,
        count(*) filter (where topic_is_confident) as confident_incidents,
        min(date_day) as first_incident,
        max(date_day) as last_incident,
        mode(offense) as modal_offense,
        mode(zone_name) as modal_zone,
        avg(dark_fraction) as avg_dark_fraction,
        count(*) filter (where any_vehicle_mo) as incidents_vehicle_mo
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and topic_id is not null
    group by topic_id
),

corpus as (
    select count(*) as topic_assigned_incidents
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and topic_id is not null
)

select
    a.topic_id,
    a.topic_id = -1 as is_noise_topic,
    w.top_words,
    w.word_count,
    w.top_word_weight,
    a.incidents,
    a.incidents * 1.0 / c.topic_assigned_incidents as share_of_assigned,
    a.confident_incidents,
    a.avg_topic_prob,
    a.modal_offense,
    a.modal_zone,
    a.avg_dark_fraction,
    a.incidents_vehicle_mo,
    a.first_incident,
    a.last_incident,
    w.topic_id is null as missing_display_words
from assigned as a
left join words as w using (topic_id)
cross join corpus as c

    where is_usable and topic_id is not null
)

    a.topic_id = -1 as is_noise_topic,
    w.top_words,
    w.word_count,
    w.top_word_weight,
    a.incidents,
    a.incidents * 1.0 / c.topic_assigned_incidents as share_of_assigned,
    a.confident_incidents,
    a.avg_topic_prob,
    a.modal_offense,
    a.modal_zone,
    a.avg_dark_fraction,
    a.incidents_vehicle_mo,
    a.first_incident,
    a.last_incident,

from assigned as a

model.opcrime_dashboard.dim_zone.raw_code:
-- One row per policing zone: geometry, who lives there, and what was reported.
--
-- Per-capita rates use the zone's own ACS population. They are not comparable to
-- a Village-wide rate computed from zone_id 0, because the tract-to-zone
-- allocation double counts residents on shared tract boundaries: the eight zone
-- populations sum to slightly more than the Village rollup. int_zone_reference
-- keeps the rollup out of this table for that reason.

with counts as (
    select
        zone_id,
        count(*) as incidents,
        count(*) filter (where is_post_regime_change) as incidents_post_regime,
        count(distinct date_day) as active_days,
        count(*) filter (where any_vehicle_mo) as incidents_vehicle_mo,
        count(*) filter (where outcome_flags_arrest) as incidents_with_arrest,
        avg(dark_fraction) as avg_dark_fraction,
        min(date_day) as first_incident,
        max(date_day) as last_incident
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable
      and zone_id is not null
    group by zone_id
)

select
    z.zone_id,
    z.zone_name,
    z.area_sq_mi,
    z.tracts_included,
    z.population,
    z.households,
    z.density_per_sq_mi,
    z.median_household_income,
    z.median_age,
    z.pct_white,
    z.pct_black,
    z.pct_asian,
    z.pct_hispanic_any_race,
    z.pct_under_18,
    z.pct_18_64,
    z.pct_65_plus,
    z.pct_owner_occupied,
    z.missing_demographics,

    coalesce(c.incidents, 0) as incidents,
    coalesce(c.incidents_post_regime, 0) as incidents_post_regime,
    coalesce(c.active_days, 0) as active_days,
    coalesce(c.incidents_vehicle_mo, 0) as incidents_vehicle_mo,
    coalesce(c.incidents_with_arrest, 0) as incidents_with_arrest,
    c.avg_dark_fraction,
    c.first_incident,
    c.last_incident,

    case when z.population > 0
         then coalesce(c.incidents, 0) * 1000.0 / z.population end
        as incidents_per_1k_residents,
    case when z.area_sq_mi > 0
         then coalesce(c.incidents, 0) / z.area_sq_mi end
        as incidents_per_sq_mi

from {{ ref('int_zone_reference') }} as z
left join counts as c using (zone_id)

model.opcrime_dashboard.stg_published_he.raw_code:
-- The published 7x24 heatmap, unpacked into one row per cell.
--
-- Read back so the cells can be compared against this project's own
-- recomputation. Agreement on the total was never enough: a weighting bug that
-- moves incidents between hours conserves the total perfectly.

with raw as (
    select content from {{ source('dashboard_panels', 'hour_dow_heatmap') }}
),

overall as (
    select cast(json_extract(s.value, '$.matrix') as double[][]) as matrix
    from raw, unnest(cast(json_extract(raw.content, '$.series') as json[])) as s(value)
    where json_extract_string(s.value, '$.key') = 'all'
)

-- DuckDB lists are 1-indexed; the published matrix is [dow][hour] zero-based.
select
    d.i - 1 as day_of_week,
    h.i - 1 as hour_of_day,
    o.matrix[d.i][h.i] as published_weight
from overall as o
cross join (select unnest(range(1, 8)) as i) as d
cross join (select unnest(range(1, 25)) as i) as h

test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_hour_dow_w.name: assert_hour_dow_weight_conserved
test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_hour_dow_w.raw_code:
{{ config(severity='error') }}

-- Every timed incident contributes exactly 1.0 of weight to the heatmap.
--
-- A range report is spread across the hours it covers, so no single cell holds a
-- whole incident, but the 168 cells together must still add up to the number of
-- incidents that went in. This caught a real bug: DuckDB's / is true division
-- even on integers, so an hour computed as start_min / 60 came out fractional,
-- the join to the hour grid missed, and 86 percent of the weight vanished while
-- the model still built cleanly. Nothing else here would have noticed.

with expected as (
    select count(*) as n
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable
      and time_parsed
      and not time_unknown_sentinel
),

actual as (
    select sum(weighted_incidents) as n
    from {{ ref('agg_incidents_by_hour_dow') }}
)

select
    e.n as expected_incidents,
    a.n as heatmap_weight,
    a.n - e.n as difference
from expected as e
cross join actual as a
where abs(a.n - e.n) > 0.001

test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_trend_mart.name: assert_trend_marts_conserve_totals
test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_trend_mart.raw_code:
-- The densified trend marts must still add up to what went into them.
--
-- Densifying a sparse series to make window functions correct means generating
-- rows, and generating rows is exactly how a grid join goes wrong: a duplicate in
-- the spine or a many-to-many join inflates every total silently, because the
-- shape of the output still looks right.
--
-- Same discipline as assert_hour_dow_weight_conserved. The transformation is
-- allowed to add zeros and nothing else, so the sum before and after must match.

with offense_expected as (
    select count(*) as n
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and offense is not null
),

offense_actual as (
    select sum(incidents) as n from {{ ref('agg_offense_trends') }}
),

topic_expected as (
    select count(*) as n
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and topic_id is not null
),

topic_actual as (
    select sum(incidents) as n from {{ ref('agg_topic_trends') }}
),

zone_expected as (
    select count(*) as n
    from {{ ref('int_incidents_enriched') }}
    where is_usable and zone_id is not null
),

zone_actual as (
    select sum(incidents) as n from {{ ref('agg_incidents_by_zone_month') }}
),

checks as (
    select 'agg_offense_trends' as mart, e.n as expected, a.n as actual
    from offense_expected as e cross join offense_actual as a
    union all
    select 'agg_topic_trends', e.n, a.n
    from topic_expected as e cross join topic_actual as a
    union all
    select 'agg_incidents_by_zone_month', e.n, a.n
    from zone_expected as e cross join zone_actual as a
)

select mart, expected, actual, actual - expected as difference
from checks
where expected <> actual

test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_zone_popul.name: assert_zone_population_rollup_consistent
test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_zone_popul.raw_code:
{{ config(severity='warn', store_failures=true) }}

-- The eight zone populations should add up to the village rollup, and they do not.
--
-- A warning by design, because this is an artifact of the method rather than a
-- mistake to fix here. Census tracts do not respect policing zone boundaries, so
-- a tract straddling two zones contributes residents to both. The sum comes out
-- slightly above the village figure.
--
-- The reason it is worth failing loudly anyway: it makes per-capita rates between
-- a zone and the village incomparable, and nothing in the numbers themselves says
-- so. A one percent tolerance catches a real regression, such as a zone being
-- allocated twice, without firing on the known overlap.

with parts as (
    select sum(population) as zone_population_sum
    from {{ ref('dim_zone') }}
),

rollup as (
    select population as village_population
    from {{ ref('stg_zone_demographics') }}
    where zone_id = 0
)

select
    p.zone_population_sum,
    r.village_population,
    p.zone_population_sum - r.village_population as difference,
    (p.zone_population_sum - r.village_population) * 100.0 / r.village_population as pct_difference
from parts as p
cross join rollup as r
where abs(p.zone_population_sum - r.village_population) * 1.0 / r.village_population > 0.01

source.opcrime_dashboard.dashboard_phase.source_description:
Outputs of this project's own Python enrichment phases, read as local Parquet.

Each phase writes to `cache/<phase>/<input_hash>/<file>.parquet` and records the
winning path in that phase's `latest.json`. Content addressing is what makes the
pipeline resumable, but it also means no dbt source can name the file directly:
a glob would union every historical run, and an absolute path would go stale and
leak the local filesystem layout into these docs.

`resolve_inputs.py` reads each `latest.json` and hardlinks the current artifact
to `dbt/inputs/<name>.parquet`. Hardlinks cost no bytes, so dbt reads the exact
file the pipeline just wrote, under a name that is stable and relative.

doc.opcrime_dashboard.__overview__.block_contents:
# Oak Park Crime Dashboard: Data Docs

This is the analytics half of a two-project chain. The
[upstream project](https://opcrime.jesse-anderson.net/dbt-docs/) scrapes PDF
activity bulletins and the village open-data dashboard, geocodes addresses, and
merges the two streams into one incident table. This project takes that table and
adds the things a question needs: time-of-day parsing, civil darkness, weather,
census denominators, keyword flags and narrative topics.

Thirty-three models, 570 documented columns, 100 tests. Everything here runs in the
nightly job. Nothing is a diagram of work happening elsewhere.

## Start here

- [data_profile_summary](#!/model/model.opcrime_dashboard.data_profile_summary)
  answers the questions people ask first. Sixteen characteristics that surprise
  people and are all correct.
- [data_quality_summary](#!/model/model.opcrime_dashboard.data_quality_summary)
  is the defect list, kept deliberately separate from the above.
- [data_parity_summary](#!/model/model.opcrime_dashboard.data_parity_summary)
  is the one to read if you only read one. It compares sixteen published figures against
  this project's own recomputation, including every heatmap cell.
- [Data Quality Report](quality.html) has the same numbers as charts.

## The shape of it

Four kinds of source feed this project:

1. **Upstream incidents** over HTTPS from the other project. The only coupling
   between the two, and deliberately the weakest available: no submodule, no
   shared database, no import. See
   [opcrime_upstream](#!/source/source.opcrime_dashboard.opcrime_upstream).
2. **This project's own Python phases**, read as local Parquet. Time parsing,
   calendar, weather, narrative flags, topics and census, each an independent
   phase with its own cache. See
   [dashboard_phases](#!/source/source.opcrime_dashboard.dashboard_phases).
3. **The published JSON panels**, read back and re-parsed. See
   [dashboard_panels](#!/source/source.opcrime_dashboard.dashboard_panels).
4. **The zone polygons** the map itself draws. See
   [dashboard_geo](#!/source/source.opcrime_dashboard.dashboard_geo).

That third one is the unusual choice. Reading back what was already published,
rather than trusting it, is what lets
[assert_coverage_parity](#!/test/test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_coverage_parity)
exist: two independent counts of the same artifacts, one in pandas and one in
SQL. All sixteen currently agree: nine row counts, and seven value checks that
compare reimplemented rules number for number rather than only in total.

## Four findings worth the click

**Reported crime tracks temperature, hard.** On hot days Oak Park averages 7.41
incidents against a 5.96 baseline, a 24 percent lift. Cold days run 20 percent
below, snowy days 19 percent below. See
[agg_weather_cohorts](#!/model/model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_weather_cohorts).
Weekends are 12 percent quieter than weekdays, which surprises most people.

**Incidents happen in the dark less often than chance would put them.** Mean
dark fraction across incidents is 0.364 against a baseline of 0.438: the average
incident falls in darkness about 7 points less than its own day's night length
would predict. Darkness is where crime is imagined, not where reporting
concentrates. See
[agg_darkness_by_offense](#!/model/model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_darkness_by_offense),
and read the caveat there about range reports before drawing conclusions per
offense.

**A third of incidents have no narrative at all.** 7,325 of 22,497 usable rows
arrive from the open-data stream as structured NIBRS charges with no prose. Every
language feature, topics and keyword flags alike, is blind to them. This is the
single most important thing to know before reading any topic number on the
dashboard, and it is why topic shares are taken over assigned narratives rather
than over all incidents.

**An exact timestamp is not an exact time.** The open-data stream carries a
precise occur_datetime, which invites reading it as a real instant. Times pile up
on round values far past anything a real distribution produces: exactly midnight
carries 55 times the uniform per-minute rate and exactly noon 50 times. Those two
are the signature of a date-only record or a form defaulting to 12:00 AM, not of
517 incidents happening at the same second. Across 44 clustered values, 4,096
incidents sit exactly on the hour, which is 30 percent of every timestamped
incident. See
[agg_time_precision](#!/model/model.opcrime_dashboard.agg_time_precision) before
trusting any hour-of-day figure to the minute.

## What the tests actually check

Coverage is 100 tests over 33 models, and a few of them earn their place:

- [assert_hour_dow_weight_conserved](#!/test/test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_hour_dow_weight_conserved)
  checks that the 168 heatmap cells sum to exactly the number of incidents that
  went in. It caught a real bug: DuckDB divides integers into floats, so an hour
  computed with a plain slash came out fractional, the join to the hour grid
  missed, and 86 percent of the weight vanished while the model still built
  clean. No other test here would have noticed.
- [assert_trend_marts_conserve_totals](#!/test/test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_trend_marts_conserve_totals)
  is the same idea applied to the monthly trend marts. Those series are densified
  so that a window function counting rows is actually counting months, and
  densifying generates rows, which is exactly how a grid join inflates a total
  without changing the shape of the output. Before the densification, 56 percent
  of the year-over-year values in agg_offense_trends did not point twelve months
  back.
- [assert_no_dead_gazetteer_flags](#!/test/test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_no_dead_gazetteer_flags)
  warns that three keyword flags never fire on any narrative in the corpus. The
  front end offers them as filters that return nothing.
- [assert_zone_population_rollup_consistent](#!/test/test.opcrime_dashboard.assert_zone_population_rollup_consistent)
  documents why a zone rate and a village rate are not comparable: census tracts
  straddle zone boundaries, so the eight zone populations sum to slightly more
  than the village total.

## Reading the numbers responsibly

Two things overlap on purpose in this project, and both will mislead anyone who
sums them.

The **weather cohorts** are not a partition. A day can be rainy and freezing and
a weekend at once, so those rows share days and their day counts do not add to
the days in range. Each cohort is only comparable to the baseline row.

The **defect and profile classes** are also not disjoint. An incident can be
ungeocoded and date-mismatched simultaneously. Where a single headline number is
wanted, count distinct records rather than adding the class counts.

And one boundary matters more than any other: **2022-01-01**. Open-data
ingestion began then. Before it, coverage is PDF bulletins only; after, it is
both streams. Every model that could mislead across that line carries an
is_post_regime_change flag so the comparison can be made like-for-like.

doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_opcrime_upstre.name: src_opcrime_upstream
doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_opcrime_upstre.block_contents:
The published output of the OP-Crime project, fetched over HTTPS from
raw.githubusercontent.com.

This is the only coupling between the two projects, and it is deliberately the
weakest one available: no submodule, no local path, no shared database, no
Python import. Pointing this dashboard at a fork of the upstream repo is a
one-line change to the `upstream_base` variable.

Both tables here are themselves modelled by a dbt project on the other side of
that boundary, so the lineage continues at
[opcrime.jesse-anderson.net/dbt-docs](https://opcrime.jesse-anderson.net/dbt-docs/).
Two graphs, one chain, joined by a URL rather than by shared state.

doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_dashboard_phas.name: src_dashboard_phases
doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_dashboard_phas.block_contents:
Outputs of this project's own Python enrichment phases, read as local Parquet.

Each phase writes to `cache/<phase>/<input_hash>/<file>.parquet` and records the
winning path in that phase's `latest.json`. Content addressing is what makes the
pipeline resumable, but it also means no dbt source can name the file directly:
a glob would union every historical run, and an absolute path would go stale and
leak the local filesystem layout into these docs.

`resolve_inputs.py` reads each `latest.json` and hardlinks the current artifact
to `dbt/inputs/<name>.parquet`. Hardlinks cost no bytes, so dbt reads the exact
file the pipeline just wrote, under a name that is stable and relative.

doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_dashboard_pane.name: src_dashboard_panels
doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_dashboard_pane.block_contents:
The precomputed JSON panels the front end downloads, read back as text and
parsed here.

Modelling the published artifact rather than recomputing it is the point. These
numbers are what a visitor actually sees, so reading them back closes the loop:
if this project's own count of usable rows disagrees with what the SPA prints,
that is a test failure with a name, not a discrepancy someone notices later.

doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_dashboard_geo.name: src_dashboard_geo
doc.opcrime_dashboard.src_dashboard_geo.block_contents:
The Oak Park policing zone polygons, read from the same GeoJSON file the SPA
downloads to draw its choropleth.

Reading the shipped file rather than a private copy means a drift between what
the map draws and what these models count shows up as a failing test here
instead of as a map that quietly disagrees with its own totals.

### Welcome!

Welcome to the auto-generated documentation for your dbt project!

### Navigation

You can use the `Project` and `Database` navigation tabs on the left side of the window to explore the models
in your project.

#### Project Tab
The `Project` tab mirrors the directory structure of your dbt project. In this tab, you can see all of the
models defined in your dbt project, as well as models imported from dbt packages.

#### Database Tab
The `Database` tab also exposes your models, but in a format that looks more like a database explorer. This view
shows relations (tables and views) grouped into database schemas. Note that ephemeral models are _not_ shown
in this interface, as they do not exist in the database.

### Graph Exploration
You can click the blue icon on the bottom-right corner of the page to view the lineage graph of your models.

On model pages, you'll see the immediate parents and children of the model you're exploring. By clicking the `Expand`
button at the top-right of this lineage pane, you'll be able to see all of the models that are used to build,
or are built from, the model you're exploring.

Once expanded, you'll be able to use the `--select` and `--exclude` model selection syntax to filter the
models in the graph. For more information on model selection, check out the [dbt docs](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/model-selection-syntax).

Note that you can also right-click on models to interactively filter and explore the graph.
